overview: This two-page unclassified airgram from the U.S. Political Adviser in Tokyo transmits a December 6, 1949, General Headquarters news release announcing revisions to Japan’s government rapeseed-collection program for the 1950 crop. Intended to stimulate domestic production amid a chronic shortage of edible oils, the revised system permitted farmers to retain part of their crop, substitute surplus rapeseed for wheat and barley delivery quotas, and receive corresponding rapeseed meal, while eliminating the return ration of rapeseed oil.

subfiles.title: Airgram from Tokyo on revisions to Japan’s rapeseed-collection program
subfiles.from: U.S. Political Adviser (USPOLAD), Tokyo; signed Sebald
subfiles.about: The airgram relays a General Headquarters news release describing changes to Japan’s rapeseed-collection rules for the 1950 crop.
subfiles.summary: The General Headquarters Public Information Office announced that Japanese farmers would be allowed to retain part of their rapeseed harvest under a revised government collection system. The reform sought to encourage domestic production and reduce Japan’s dependence on imported edible oils. Prefectural production, retention, and delivery amounts would be assigned by the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry; farmers could substitute rapeseed for wheat and barley quotas at a specified rate and would receive corresponding rapeseed meal, but no return ration of rapeseed oil.

interest: The airgram provides a compact account of how occupation-era authorities and the Japanese government attempted to correct an unpopular compulsory-collection system while addressing a serious edible-oil shortage. Its precise substitution rate and description of benefits returned to producers make it useful for studying agricultural rationing, incentive policy, and food-supply management in early postwar Japan. It also illustrates how General Headquarters publicized economic reforms through USPOLAD reporting channels.
